newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain law to increase regional financial stability.
newsitem.headline: Spain law to increase regional financial stability.

text.p: The fast-growing pile of Spanish municipal debt may soon stop accumulating as regional governments' new tax collection rights help them shore up budgets, analysts say.

Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government has accompanied the 1997 budget with a new law designed to give the 17 regions more freedom on expenditures and revenues, increasing their ability to repay debt.
"With the new system we will likely see an improvement in the state of local finance," said Juan Jose Garcia, director at Standard & Poor's in Madrid.
Spanish regional debt had mushroomed to 4.261 trillion pesetas by the end of June 1996 from 945 billion pesetas at the end of 1990.

"It is pretty normal to see an increase in expenses at the regional level when fiscal policy becomes stricter at the central level," said Juergen Von Hagen, professor at Mannheim University. "That was the case of Spain in the past."

The centre-right minority government, which depends for a parliamentary majority on its allies from Catalonia and the Canary Islands, is set to approve a new law which will shift up to 30 percent of income tax revenue directly to the regions within two years.

Analysts are convinced that the new regulatory framework will make regional governments more virtuous, enabling them to curtail deficits and ensure Spain can meet to the stringent criteria for joining in the launch of Europe's single currency.

To particiate in the planned 1999 Euro debut, Spain must meet requirements on interest rates, exchange rates, debt levels, inflation and on the public sector deficit, which includes the heavy burden of regional debt.
Spain has said its public sector budget deficit would decline to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from a projected 4.4 percent this year and 6.6 percent last year.
"The new system will be more transparent. Every single local government has to show how much they spend and how they fund it," S&P's Garcia said.
From 1998 on, all 17 regional governments will have acquired scope to change tax rates by up to six percent. They will also assume total responsibility for education and health expenses.
"The new system will be positive for the local governments. Only Andalucia and Extremadura voted against it, while all the others were in favour," said Federico Mayoria, analyst at Ibca in Barcelona.
But not all analysts agreed. Roberto Centeno, economics professor at Universidad Politecnica in Madrid, said that the rich will get richer and the poor, poorer.
"The new system leaves behind almost every trace of solidarity among regions," he said. "And we, as Spaniards, never voted to shift towards a federalist setup."
Even worse for prospective investors is the possible duplication of public administration involved in the new financing scheme, which could push regional deficits higher.
"Since 1980-1981 the overall number of public employees has increased by more than 50 percent," Centeno said.
"It is hard to prove but if you compare this trend to the other European countries', the only possible reason for such a rise is federalism," he added.
